extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of architectural history; scholars and practitioners identifying/ dating Venetian Byzantine and Gothic architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Use carved capitals, leaf treatment, archivolt and cornice mouldings, and traceries to identify the stylistic period and date Venetian buildings (Byzantine, transitional, early Gothic, late Gothic). The page gives features to inspect (profiles, abaci, mouldings, material, leaf execution) and how they function as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaf form on capitals (loss of Corinthian volute / 'pure' leaves)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaves which have lost the Corinthian volute and are 'pure and plain leaves' (as used in Lombardic Gothic of the early thirteenth century) are diagnostic of that early Gothic/transitional period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare fig. 13 (pure plain leaves) and the Lombardic Gothic examples; presence of these plain, pointed leaves across mouldings/windows is used to fix an early date (examples: Campo Sta. Ma. Mater Domini, Casa Cicogna).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enrichment of leaf surfaces (ribbed/pointed/carved ornament)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaves enriched by carving each surface into a 'beautifid ribbed and pointed leaf' indicate a later, richer Gothic development compared with plain leaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: fig. 6 is fig. 13 'so enriched'; such enrichment (surface ribs, projections) is characteristic of the later 13th/early 14th-century Venetian capitals (see figs. 9 and 12 for noble development).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaf execution technique (raised edge, central rib, drill-holes, furrows)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific cutting techniques—leaf cut into the stone with a raised edge and a raised rib up the centre; sharp furrow from root to point; deep drill-holes between points—are diagnostic features of particular dates and schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare figs. 2, 4, 5, 7, 10, 11: e.g., fig. 2 (Egyptian bas-relief style with raised edge and central rib), fig. 3 (drill holes between points), fig. 10 (three ribs on upper surface). These micro-features help distinguish early/archaic from later/naturalistic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence or absence of a central rib on leaves
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a leaf has a rib (central raised ridge) or merely a sharp raised ridge/no rib helps distinguish levels of finish and period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: fig. 5 (central capital of Casa Falier) has no rib but a sharp raised ridge; later examples add a rib in the centre (fig. 5 advanced condition). Note lobing shapes (round middle, truncated sides) as additional clues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nodding leaves versus curled 'ball' extremities (naturalism vs late Gothic intemperance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaves that simply bend, wave and nod are signs of healthy, earlier naturalism; leaves whose extremities curl completely round into a 'ball' indicate late Gothic excess (loss of life, intemperance) and a later date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual judgment: curling/ball-form is described as a 'fatal symptom' and used widely in later Venetian Gothic (ball of coiled leafage grows in complexity; see figs. 11, 14). Use presence of coiled leaf-balls as an indicator of later (post-early fourteenth-century) work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital profile curvature and abacus form as dating tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall profile shapes (concave on angles, slightly convex at sides; subtle curvatures) and the design of the abacus (e.g., reduplications of dentilled mouldings) are reliable indicators of early Byzantine/transitional date or of later Gothic forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: profile with four reduplications of the dentilled mouldings of St. Mark's is an 'unfailing test of early date'; fig. 8 profile described as 'curiously subtle' (concave on angles). Compare profiles i, 1h, k etc. in Plate X series to establish fellowship and date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of profile series (fellowship of profiles) for chronological placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Matching a capital's or moulding's profile to a series of known profiles (Byzantine, transitional, Gothic) establishes stylistic fellowship and therefore helps date the element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author compares rows of profiles (e.g., 2a to k, i to k) and uses similarities to tie the Ducal Palace work to earlier Byzantine examples. Match your specimen to the plate-series profiles (noted by letters/numbers) to infer date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abacus profile rounding (top vs bottom of cavetto) as date marker
rubrics_metrics.description: Byzantine abaci tend to be rounded at the bottom of the cavetto (if at all), whereas late Gothic abaci are rounded at the top of the cavetto; this difference is a useful test of date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Plate X rows: Byzantine (examples 7,8,9,10,20,28,46) vs late Gothic examples (52–56). Use direct comparison (e.g., 28 vs 29) to test antiquity of a building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contraction of the abacus through time
rubrics_metrics.description: The gradual contraction (narrowing) of the abacus over successive profiles indicates chronological change toward later, weaker forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare early forms (e.g., 4c from Murano) with later forms (4e) to observe progressive contraction; contraction correlates with later (post-1350/1380) periods and decline of form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archivolt moulding composition and construction (two-slab method, soffit/face treatments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Byzantine archivolts are commonly built of two slabs of marble (one for the soffit, another for the face) with the soffit stone worked on the edge into a roll or dentil and the face stone bordered and let edgeways into the wall; richer archivolts add a cornice and sculptured faces/soffits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Profiles 1–11 in Plate VIII illustrate this; sculptured soffits and concavities (figs. 1,2,4,5,6) indicate Byzantine workmanship. Absence of the soffit stone or translation into brick indicates transitional/early Gothic changes (see figs. 13–14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material of moulding (brick vs stone) as a transitional indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Brick mouldings (flat brick mouldings) are characteristic of the transitional period and are attempts to imitate the flat sculptured archivolts of Byzantine times; stone translations of those brick profiles form the universal archivolt of early Gothic Venice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figs. 13 and 14 (Plate VIII) show the first brick mouldings of the transitional period; compare brick group (3–11) with later stone groups (14–18, 17–18 cavetto additions) to place chronology and function (doors vs windows).

rubrics_metrics.name: Archivolts incomplete on both sides (one-sided/indoor mouldings) vs fully developed double-sided mouldings
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Venetian archivolts assume an outside view only and are incomplete on their inner face; archivolts that are complete on both sides indicate a more fully developed Gothic system and an architecturally mature building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most archivolts in the plates are 'indoors mouldings' (one-sided); examples of both-sided mouldings occur in the Ducal Palace (profiles 28, 31) and in the Frari (profile 35, complete arch moulding). Use presence/absence of a back-side moulding to infer architectural completeness and date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific moulding ornaments (dog-tooth, gabled dentil, cavetto depth, beading) identify window order and period
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornaments such as dog-tooth under the dentil, gabled dentil, added cavetto depth, beading/truncation of angles all mark particular window orders and stages of Gothic development (early, intermediate, late).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: dog-tooth additions in early fourth-order windows (fig. 20); gabled dentil (fig. 21); intermediate groups (25–28) are rare and often localized to Ducal Palace or Frari. The 'established moulding' for later windows is profile 29.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cornice/plinth uses and profile comparisons as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Cornices and running plinths occur in many proportions and uses (true cornices, window-sills, dripstones). Their profiles and their direct resemblance across buildings help confirm early dates and stylistic relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plate X rows 1–24 show Byzantine plinths; compare running plinths (Casa Loredan 25) with abaci of large shafts (50) — the moulding remains largely the same while proportions change. Byzantine cornices with nodding acanthus may indicate Byzantine origin of later Gothic cornices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traceries treated as part of a larger composition (cut from a 'colossal piece' of marble lace)
rubrics_metrics.description: Venetian traceries are often planned as part of an indefinitely extending pattern and then cut to window shape; terminal quatrefoils and foliation are frequently cut off at the flanks—unlike Northern Gothic traceries which are individually planned to fit a single window.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for traceries where quatrefoils are truncated at window edges and terminal mouldings consume part of a quatrefoil; this 'diaper' approach is a hallmark of Venetian practice (examples: Porta della Carta, Casa Bernardo, Ducal Palace traceries). Use this to distinguish Venetian from Northern Gothic tracery logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of small-scale leaf/leaf-lobe details (furrows, divisions, ribs) to track advance of Gothic naturalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in how furrows, ribs and lobe separations are treated (from sharp furrows to shallower furrows and more flexible lobes) mark the forty-year interval of principal Gothic advance (roughly early to mid-14th century).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare fig. 1 (sharp furrow to point), fig. 6 (sharp furrow drawn only to central lobe, rest left nearly flat), fig. 7 (sharper furrows soften), figs. 10–12 (movement to full Gothic naturalism). The sequence from fig. 10 to figs. 11 and 12 shows the main extent of change.
